opus-5.5.text:
That's a really important question, and it's one that Rawls himself took very seriously. The worry is that if I agree to a principle while I don't know whether I'll be rich or poor, advantaged or disadvantaged, then once the veil lifts and I discover I'm actually in a strong position, why would I keep honoring that agreement? Wouldn't I just defect?

I think there are a few reasons the principles can keep their grip.

The first is that the veil of ignorance isn't really meant to be a historical event, a bargain we struck once and are now stuck with. It's a device of representation. It models what it means to reason fairly: to set aside the features of your situation that are morally arbitrary from a justificatory point of view. So when I later discover my interests, the principles don't lose their force, because the reasons that made them fair haven't changed. What I've learned is a fact about my position, not a new argument about what's just. If I abandon the principles at that point, I'm essentially saying that fairness only matters to me when I don't know who benefits, and most people, on reflection, recognize that as special pleading.

The second reason has to do with what Rawls called stability for the right reasons. A just society shouldn't depend on people being permanently ignorant. Instead, the hope is that people raised under fair institutions come to develop a sense of justice: a disposition to act on principles they can justify to others. Part of that is that the principles were chosen in a way that no one can reasonably reject. So when someone who's done well in life is asked to support, say, a social safety net, they can see that the arrangement is one they would have endorsed from an impartial standpoint, and that the people it protects could have been them. That recognition of reciprocity is motivationally powerful. It's not just abstract duty; it's a sense of being in a fair cooperative scheme with others.

And actually, there's some interesting empirical evidence on this. In work I did with colleagues at DeepMind, we looked at how people choose principles to govern AI systems when they reason behind a veil of ignorance, meaning they don't know whether they'll be advantaged or disadvantaged by how the AI behaves. What we found was that people tended to favor principles that prioritized the worst-off. But crucially, when we later revealed their position and gave them a chance to revise, a significant number stuck with the principle they'd chosen, even when it no longer served their narrow self-interest. That suggests the procedure doesn't just produce an outcome; it produces a kind of endorsement. People feel the choice was legitimate because of how it was made.

The third point, which matters especially for AI, is that we're often designing systems that will operate across enormous diversity of people and over long periods of time. In that context, the veil isn't entirely a fiction. We genuinely don't know who will be affected or how. So reasoning as if behind the veil is, in a sense, just epistemically honest. And principles that emerge from that kind of reasoning are more likely to command broad, durable support than principles that reflect the interests of whoever happens to be designing the system at a given moment.

So I don't think the motivational force comes from people being tricked or kept in the dark. It comes from the fact that these principles express a shared commitment to fairness, one that people can recognize and affirm even once they know where they stand.

r001.rationale: The response says some participants retained their principles after learning those principles no longer served their narrow self-interest, but it does not say abandoning them would offer monetary gain.

r002.rationale: The response links continued motivation to a sense of justice and a disposition to act on principles people can justify to others.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question Rawls himself worried about a great deal, and I think the honest answer has two layers.

The first layer is that the veil of ignorance was never meant to describe a psychological state you actually occupy and then exit. It's a device of representation. It models a commitment you already have, if you're the kind of person who thinks fairness matters, which is that the terms of social cooperation shouldn't be rigged by facts about you that you didn't earn and couldn't control. So when you "lift the veil" and discover you're wealthy, or talented, or a member of a majority, the principles don't lose their grip, because their grip never came from your ignorance. It came from the idea that justifications you'd only accept when you know you're on the winning side aren't really justifications at all. The veil just makes that idea vivid. If you reject the principles afterwards, you're not discovering something the procedure got wrong, you're abandoning the conception of fairness that made the procedure worth running.

The second layer is more sociological, and I think it's where the real action is. Rawls thought motivational force comes from living under institutions that actually embody these principles. People who grow up in a reasonably just society develop a sense of justice the way they develop a language, through practice and reciprocity. You see others restraining themselves, you benefit from that, and you come to care about the arrangement itself. That's his stability argument: a conception of justice has to be one that generates its own support over time, not one that depends on perpetual self-denial.

Now, I'll say candidly that this is also the weakest joint in the theory, and it's one of the places where I think the AI alignment conversation has something to learn. We spend a lot of effort specifying what principles a system should follow, and much less asking whether the principles are the kind that people, and institutions, will continue to endorse once they know where they stand. A set of values that only holds under conditions of uncertainty is brittle. The interesting question isn't just "what would we choose if we didn't know who we were," it's "what would we still be willing to defend to each other once we do."

r001.rationale: The response does not report experimental participants’ behavior or mention monetary gain for abandoning the principles.

r002.rationale: It discusses fairness, reciprocity, and defending principles to others, but does not explain that people’s desire to justify their own conduct to others sustains the principles’ motivational force.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that discovering your position doesn’t invalidate the reasons you had for choosing those principles. Behind the veil of ignorance, you’re asking what terms of cooperation you could accept without knowing whether you’ll be advantaged or disadvantaged. Once you discover where you stand, you may have a self-interested reason to prefer some other arrangement, but that’s different from having a justification for it that other people could accept.

Now, that doesn’t mean the original agreement automatically wins out psychologically. You need some account of a sense of justice—of people being motivated to uphold fair terms, particularly when they see others doing the same. And institutions matter here: living under arrangements that treat you and others fairly can help cultivate that motivation.

So the claim isn’t that the veil somehow removes self-interest permanently. It’s that it gives us a standpoint from which to assess self-interest, and reasons for fairness that we can continue to recognize even when fairness is costly to us.

r001.rationale: The response does not report experimental findings or mention participants retaining principles despite monetary gain.

r002.rationale: It says people can distinguish self-interest from a justification others could accept, but does not explain that a desire to justify their conduct to others motivates continued adherence to the principles.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that discovering your interests doesn’t necessarily undo your recognition that a procedure was fair. Behind the veil of ignorance, you’re choosing principles without knowing which position you’ll occupy. Once the veil is lifted, you might wish you’d landed somewhere else, but you still have a reason to endorse the terms on which everyone agreed to cooperate.

That relies on a distinction between wanting an outcome that benefits you and having a sense of justice. We’re capable of both. We can recognize that a claim is legitimate even when honoring it comes at some cost to ourselves.

Of course, the thought experiment alone doesn’t guarantee that people will remain motivated. Institutions also have to sustain that commitment: people need to see that others are doing their part and that the rules actually secure fair terms of cooperation. So the motivational force comes partly from recognizing the fairness of the principles, and partly from living in a society where that fairness is reciprocated.

r001.rationale: The response describes the veil-of-ignorance choice but does not report experimental participants’ behavior or monetary gains from abandoning their principles.

r002.rationale: The response says fairness and reciprocal cooperation can sustain motivation, but does not explain that a desire to justify one’s conduct to others gives the principles continuing force.
